deprecated"}],"state":"closed","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":26,"created_at":"2023-05-29T10:56:25Z","updated_at":"2024-12-01T15:55:12Z","closed_at":"2024-12-01T15:20:56Z","author_association":"MEMBER","active_lock_reason":null,"body":"The returns for several quadrature methods are from a time long-gone by, when switching output signature based on arguments was considered acceptable. Also, there are other issues to fix, like not returning enough information in all cases.

Quoting @WarrenWeckesser from #7816:
> The return values of `quad` is another one of those ugly warts in the scipy API.
> 
> The number of return values depends on the argument `full_output`, and on whether or not the algorithm converges.

As of 1.10.1, the returns looks like this (though it's not the fully story even):
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c1ed5ece8ffbf05356a22a8106affcd11bd3aee0/scipy/integrate/_quadpack_py.py#L505-L513

#7816 was tackled in #18298 in an output-compatible way, i.e. returns would have retained their shape as a 5-tuple if `full_output=True` and a 2-tuple if `full_output=False` (even though enhanced by being a `Bunch` that just fakes being a 2-tuple), where the `full_output=True` case would have looked something like this:
```
Real:    QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict=infodict, message=message, explain=explain)
Complex: QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict}, message={"real": real_message, "imag":imag_message}, explain={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict})
```

I think this is disadvantageous on several points, e.g. the nesting of the dicts for complex, the divergence between real & complex, the massive extent of infodict. #18298 ended up not being merged for 1.11, and some of the other work that had happened already (#17837, #17964) was reverted last-minute in #18560. I'm grateful for @mdhaber and @j-bowhay for allowing more time on this topic, and apologize for delaying this. 

I believe we should use our "breakage budget" to change this API _once_ for the foreseeable future, and not introduce something now that we're not happy with for the next 5-10 years at least.

My thoughts on the API design are as follows:
* We need to move away completely from mutable return signature, even if we need to wait until SciPy 2.0 to remove it completely.
  * This can be done by introducing a `legacy` keyword that starts as being `True` (but raising a deprecation warning) and does
    ```
    if legacy:
        return ...  #  as current signature: y, abserr, infodict, message, explain
    else:
        return ...  # new signature, to be determined
    ```
  * we can change the default to `legacy=False` after 2 releases
* shape of the result type: dictionary wrapped in a special class? This is the `Bunch`-approach, but perhaps can be changed further
  * One approach is to package _everything_ into (say) `QuadResult`, including the integral itself. This is what #18298 was doing, and is a fine approach
  * My suspicion however is that >90% of the use-cases for `quad` are still just "get me the integral", so I think it might be interesting to consider a signature:
    ```
    return y, QuadInfo(...)
    ```
    which would allow people to easily discard the information if they don't need it (e.g. `result, _ = quad(...)`), rather than having to learn how to extract this from `QuadInfo` (if they're not interested in it).
* Dealing with the complex case. I think we should have _the same_ structure in `QuadResult` /  `QuadInfo` regardless of whether we have real or complex integrals. The choice then comes down to whether we nest the imaginary part as an optional field in the result, or whether we do something like `.real` / `.imag`, where real is always populated, and `.imag` might be missing.
  * Option A:
    ```
    QuadResult(..., imag=QuadResult, ...)
    ```
  * Option B:
    ```
    QuadResult(.real.<key>=value, .imag.<key>=value)
    ```
  * Option C: something else?
* fully unpack & enrich content - in particular, I think we should not be giving back error flags anywhere.
  * For example, we should be able to replace the following with something better:
    > `ierlst`: A rank-1 integer array of length ``M_f`` containing an error flag corresponding to the interval in the same position in `infodict['rslist']`.  See the explanation dictionary (last entry in the output tuple) for the meaning of the codes. 
  * I'd also like to get rid of the following kind of instructions. I think we should just compute useful information and make it easily accessible. If we want to save performance and write a separate result class, we can even do this lazily.
    > Let I be the sequence `infodict['iord']` and let E be the sequence `infodict['elist']`.  Then `E[I[1]], ..., E[I[L]]` forms a decreasing sequence.
* size/structure of current `infodict`. The current infodict is a mess of different fields which are all pretty illegible. I would fundamentally reshuffle these and provide a nicer interface for them. @mdhaber had the idea of not packing everything from infodict into our new result type right away, but staying minimal and seeing if people complain that something's missing. That sounds like a good approach to me. Besides the question of when or if we introduce given fields in the result, I'd like to organize them in ways that make sense based on their information (e.g. about the nodes, the weights, the intervals). 

I came up with a quick draft in #18298 from looking at the docstrings (adapted slightly here), but I'm certain this can and should be refined. It's just here for illustrative purposes for now, all the sections and their content are up for bikeshedding.
```
QuadInfo: {
    # errors (should this be a dict or part of `'integration'`?)
    'abserr': ...
    # basics about eval
    'integration': {
      'neval': ...,
      'last': ...,
      # perhaps enriched by...
      'routine': # name of the quadpack routine that was called
      <crucial input kwargs>
    },
    # nested QuadResult for imaginary component, if complex_func
    'imag': None or QuadResult,
    # details
    'subintervals': {
        # all relevant information about subintervals (suitably renamed if we want),
        # e.g. replacing alist, blist, rlist, elist, iord for finite integration
        # resp. lst, rslst, erlst, ierlst for infinite integration
    },
    'break_points': None or {
        # equivalents of pts, level, ndin, if points kwarg was provided (else None)
    },
    'weights': None or {
        # reflect weight & wvar kwargs for completeness (if provided, else the whole thing is None)
        # plus extra info for sin/cos weights, if applicable.
    },
    'moments': None or {
        # momcom, nnlog, chebmo
    }
}

deprecated"}],"state":"closed","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":29,"created_at":"2023-05-29T10:56:25Z","updated_at":"2024-12-01T17:14:02Z","closed_at":"2024-12-01T15:20:56Z","author_association":"MEMBER","active_lock_reason":null,"body":"The returns for several quadrature methods are from a time long-gone by, when switching output signature based on arguments was considered acceptable. Also, there are other issues to fix, like not returning enough information in all cases.

Quoting @WarrenWeckesser from #7816:
> The return values of `quad` is another one of those ugly warts in the scipy API.
> 
> The number of return values depends on the argument `full_output`, and on whether or not the algorithm converges.

As of 1.10.1, the returns looks like this (though it's not the fully story even):
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c1ed5ece8ffbf05356a22a8106affcd11bd3aee0/scipy/integrate/_quadpack_py.py#L505-L513

#7816 was tackled in #18298 in an output-compatible way, i.e. returns would have retained their shape as a 5-tuple if `full_output=True` and a 2-tuple if `full_output=False` (even though enhanced by being a `Bunch` that just fakes being a 2-tuple), where the `full_output=True` case would have looked something like this:
```
Real:    QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict=infodict, message=message, explain=explain)
Complex: QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict}, message={"real": real_message, "imag":imag_message}, explain={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict})
```

I think this is disadvantageous on several points, e.g. the nesting of the dicts for complex, the divergence between real & complex, the massive extent of infodict. #18298 ended up not being merged for 1.11, and some of the other work that had happened already (#17837, #17964) was reverted last-minute in #18560. I'm grateful for @mdhaber and @j-bowhay for allowing more time on this topic, and apologize for delaying this. 

I believe we should use our "breakage budget" to change this API _once_ for the foreseeable future, and not introduce something now that we're not happy with for the next 5-10 years at least.

My thoughts on the API design are as follows:
* We need to move away completely from mutable return signature, even if we need to wait until SciPy 2.0 to remove it completely.
  * This can be done by introducing a `legacy` keyword that starts as being `True` (but raising a deprecation warning) and does
    ```
    if legacy:
        return ...  #  as current signature: y, abserr, infodict, message, explain
    else:
        return ...  # new signature, to be determined
    ```
  * we can change the default to `legacy=False` after 2 releases
* shape of the result type: dictionary wrapped in a special class? This is the `Bunch`-approach, but perhaps can be changed further
  * One approach is to package _everything_ into (say) `QuadResult`, including the integral itself. This is what #18298 was doing, and is a fine approach
  * My suspicion however is that >90% of the use-cases for `quad` are still just "get me the integral", so I think it might be interesting to consider a signature:
    ```
    return y, QuadInfo(...)
    ```
    which would allow people to easily discard the information if they don't need it (e.g. `result, _ = quad(...)`), rather than having to learn how to extract this from `QuadInfo` (if they're not interested in it).
* Dealing with the complex case. I think we should have _the same_ structure in `QuadResult` /  `QuadInfo` regardless of whether we have real or complex integrals. The choice then comes down to whether we nest the imaginary part as an optional field in the result, or whether we do something like `.real` / `.imag`, where real is always populated, and `.imag` might be missing.
  * Option A:
    ```
    QuadResult(..., imag=QuadResult, ...)
    ```
  * Option B:
    ```
    QuadResult(.real.<key>=value, .imag.<key>=value)
    ```
  * Option C: something else?
* fully unpack & enrich content - in particular, I think we should not be giving back error flags anywhere.
  * For example, we should be able to replace the following with something better:
    > `ierlst`: A rank-1 integer array of length ``M_f`` containing an error flag corresponding to the interval in the same position in `infodict['rslist']`.  See the explanation dictionary (last entry in the output tuple) for the meaning of the codes. 
  * I'd also like to get rid of the following kind of instructions. I think we should just compute useful information and make it easily accessible. If we want to save performance and write a separate result class, we can even do this lazily.
    > Let I be the sequence `infodict['iord']` and let E be the sequence `infodict['elist']`.  Then `E[I[1]], ..., E[I[L]]` forms a decreasing sequence.
* size/structure of current `infodict`. The current infodict is a mess of different fields which are all pretty illegible. I would fundamentally reshuffle these and provide a nicer interface for them. @mdhaber had the idea of not packing everything from infodict into our new result type right away, but staying minimal and seeing if people complain that something's missing. That sounds like a good approach to me. Besides the question of when or if we introduce given fields in the result, I'd like to organize them in ways that make sense based on their information (e.g. about the nodes, the weights, the intervals). 

I came up with a quick draft in #18298 from looking at the docstrings (adapted slightly here), but I'm certain this can and should be refined. It's just here for illustrative purposes for now, all the sections and their content are up for bikeshedding.
```
QuadInfo: {
    # errors (should this be a dict or part of `'integration'`?)
    'abserr': ...
    # basics about eval
    'integration': {
      'neval': ...,
      'last': ...,
      # perhaps enriched by...
      'routine': # name of the quadpack routine that was called
      <crucial input kwargs>
    },
    # nested QuadResult for imaginary component, if complex_func
    'imag': None or QuadResult,
    # details
    'subintervals': {
        # all relevant information about subintervals (suitably renamed if we want),
        # e.g. replacing alist, blist, rlist, elist, iord for finite integration
        # resp. lst, rslst, erlst, ierlst for infinite integration
    },
    'break_points': None or {
        # equivalents of pts, level, ndin, if points kwarg was provided (else None)
    },
    'weights': None or {
        # reflect weight & wvar kwargs for completeness (if provided, else the whole thing is None)
        # plus extra info for sin/cos weights, if applicable.
    },
    'moments': None or {
        # momcom, nnlog, chebmo

returns for several quadrature methods are from a time long-gone by, when switching output signature based on arguments was considered acceptable. Also, there are other issues to fix, like not returning enough information in all cases.

Quoting @WarrenWeckesser from #7816:
> The return values of `quad` is another one of those ugly warts in the scipy API.
> 
> The number of return values depends on the argument `full_output`, and on whether or not the algorithm converges.

As of 1.10.1, the returns looks like this (though it's not the fully story even):
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/c1ed5ece8ffbf05356a22a8106affcd11bd3aee0/scipy/integrate/_quadpack_py.py#L505-L513

#7816 was tackled in #18298 in an output-compatible way, i.e. returns would have retained their shape as a 5-tuple if `full_output=True` and a 2-tuple if `full_output=False` (even though enhanced by being a `Bunch` that just fakes being a 2-tuple), where the `full_output=True` case would have looked something like this:
```
Real:    QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict=infodict, message=message, explain=explain)
Complex: QuadResult(integral, abserr, infodict={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict}, message={"real": real_message, "imag":imag_message}, explain={"real": real_infodict, "imag":imag_infodict})
```

I think this is disadvantageous on several points, e.g. the nesting of the dicts for complex, the divergence between real & complex, the massive extent of infodict. #18298 ended up not being merged for 1.11, and some of the other work that had happened already (#17837, #17964) was reverted last-minute in #18560. I'm grateful for @mdhaber and @j-bowhay for allowing more time on this topic, and apologize for delaying this. 

I believe we should use our "breakage budget" to change this API _once_ for the foreseeable future, and not introduce something now that we're not happy with for the next 5-10 years at least.

My thoughts on the API design are as follows:
* We need to move away completely from mutable return signature, even if we need to wait until SciPy 2.0 to remove it completely.
  * This can be done by introducing a `legacy` keyword that starts as being `True` (but raising a deprecation warning) and does
    ```
    if legacy:
        return ...  #  as current signature: y, abserr, infodict, message, explain
    else:
        return ...  # new signature, to be determined
    ```
  * we can change the default to `legacy=False` after 2 releases
* shape of the result type: dictionary wrapped in a special class? This is the `Bunch`-approach, but perhaps can be changed further
  * One approach is to package _everything_ into (say) `QuadResult`, including the integral itself. This is what #18298 was doing, and is a fine approach
  * My suspicion however is that >90% of the use-cases for `quad` are still just "get me the integral", so I think it might be interesting to consider a signature:
    ```
    return y, QuadInfo(...)
    ```
    which would allow people to easily discard the information if they don't need it (e.g. `result, _ = quad(...)`), rather than having to learn how to extract this from `QuadInfo` (if they're not interested in it).
* Dealing with the complex case. I think we should have _the same_ structure in `QuadResult` /  `QuadInfo` regardless of whether we have real or complex integrals. The choice then comes down to whether we nest the imaginary part as an optional field in the result, or whether we do something like `.real` / `.imag`, where real is always populated, and `.imag` might be missing.
  * Option A:
    ```
    QuadResult(..., imag=QuadResult, ...)
    ```
  * Option B:
    ```
    QuadResult(.real.<key>=value, .imag.<key>=value)
    ```
  * Option C: something else?
* fully unpack & enrich content - in particular, I think we should not be giving back error flags anywhere.
  * For example, we should be able to replace the following with something better:
    > `ierlst`: A rank-1 integer array of length ``M_f`` containing an error flag corresponding to the interval in the same position in `infodict['rslist']`.  See the explanation dictionary (last entry in the output tuple) for the meaning of the codes. 
  * I'd also like to get rid of the following kind of instructions. I think we should just compute useful information and make it easily accessible. If we want to save performance and write a separate result class, we can even do this lazily.
    > Let I be the sequence `infodict['iord']` and let E be the sequence `infodict['elist']`.  Then `E[I[1]], ..., E[I[L]]` forms a decreasing sequence.
* size/structure of current `infodict`. The current infodict is a mess of different fields which are all pretty illegible. I would fundamentally reshuffle these and provide a nicer interface for them. @mdhaber had the idea of not packing everything from infodict into our new result type right away, but staying minimal and seeing if people complain that something's missing. That sounds like a good approach to me. Besides the question of when or if we introduce given fields in the result, I'd like to organize them in ways that make sense based on their information (e.g. about the nodes, the weights, the intervals). 

I came up with a quick draft in #18298 from looking at the docstrings (adapted slightly here), but I'm certain this can and should be refined. It's just here for illustrative purposes for now, all the sections and their content are up for bikeshedding.
```
QuadInfo: {
    # errors (should this be a dict or part of `'integration'`?)
    'abserr': ...
    # basics about eval
    'integration': {
      'neval': ...,
      'last': ...,
      # perhaps enriched by...
      'routine': # name of the quadpack routine that was called
      <crucial input kwargs>
    },
    # nested QuadResult for imaginary component, if complex_func
    'imag': None or QuadResult,
    # details
    'subintervals': {
        # all relevant information about subintervals (suitably renamed if we want),
        # e.g. replacing alist, blist, rlist, elist, iord for finite integration
        # resp. lst, rslst, erlst, ierlst for infinite integration
    },
    'break_points': None or {
        # equivalents of pts, level, ndin, if points kwarg was provided (else None)
    },
    'weights': None or {
        # reflect weight & wvar kwargs for completeness (if provided, else the whole thing is None)
        # plus extra info for sin/cos weights, if applicable.
    },
    'moments': None or {
        # momcom, nnlog, chebmo
    }
}

TL;DR: The way we build against numpy has changed as of numpy 2.0. This bot
PR has updated the recipe to account for the changes (see below for details).

The biggest change is that we no longer need to use the oldest available numpy
version at build time in order to support old numpy version at runtime - numpy
will by default use a compatible ABI for the oldest still-supported numpy versions.

Additionally, we no longer need to use `{{ pin_compatible("numpy") }}` as a
run requirement - this has been handled for more than two years now by a
run-export on the numpy package itself. The migrator will therefore remove
any occurrences of this.

However, you will still need to add the lower bound for the numpy version,
in line with what the upstream package requires. The default lower bound from
the run-export is `>=1.19`; if your package needs a newer version than that,
please add `numpy >=x.y` under `run:`.

Finally, by default, building against numpy 2.0 will assume that the package
is compatible with numpy 2.0, which is not necessarily the case. You should
check that the upstream package explicitly supports numpy 2.0, otherwise you
need to add a `- numpy <2.0dev0` run requirement until that happens (check numpy
issue 26191 for an overview of the most important packages).

### To-Dos:
  * [ ] Match run-requirements for numpy (i.e. check upstream `pyproject.toml` or however the project specifies numpy compatibility)
    * If upstream is not yet compatible with numpy 2.0, add `numpy <2.0dev0` upper bound under `run:`.
    * If upstream is already compatible with numpy 2.0, double-check their supported numpy versions.
    * If upstream requires a minimum numpy version newer than 1.19, you need to add `numpy >=x.y` under `run:`.
  * [ ] Remove any remaining occurrences of `{{ pin_compatible("numpy") }}` that the bot may have missed.

PS. If the build does not compile anymore, this is almost certainly a sign that
the upstream project is not yet ready for numpy 2.0; do not close this PR until
a version compatible with numpy 2.0 has been released upstream and on this
feedstock (in the meantime, you can keep the bot from reopening this PR in

TL;DR: The way we build against numpy has changed as of numpy 2.0. This bot
PR has updated the recipe to account for the changes (see below for details).

The biggest change is that we no longer need to use the oldest available numpy
version at build time in order to support old numpy version at runtime - numpy
will by default use a compatible ABI for the oldest still-supported numpy versions.

Additionally, we no longer need to use `{{ pin_compatible("numpy") }}` as a
run requirement - this has been handled for more than two years now by a
run-export on the numpy package itself. The migrator will therefore remove
any occurrences of this.

However, you will still need to add the lower bound for the numpy version,
in line with what the upstream package requires. The default lower bound from
the run-export is `>=1.19`; if your package needs a newer version than that,
please add `numpy >=x.y` under `run:`.

Finally, by default, building against numpy 2.0 will assume that the package
is compatible with numpy 2.0, which is not necessarily the case. You should
check that the upstream package explicitly supports numpy 2.0, otherwise you
need to add a `- numpy <2.0dev0` run requirement until that happens (check numpy
issue 26191 for an overview of the most important packages).

### To-Dos:
  * [ ] Match run-requirements for numpy (i.e. check upstream `pyproject.toml` or however the project specifies numpy compatibility)
    * If upstream is not yet compatible with numpy 2.0, add `numpy <2.0dev0` upper bound under `run:`.
    * If upstream is already compatible with numpy 2.0, double-check their supported numpy versions.
    * If upstream requires a minimum numpy version newer than 1.19, you need to add `numpy >=x.y` under `run:`.
  * [ ] Remove any remaining occurrences of `{{ pin_compatible("numpy") }}` that the bot may have missed.

PS. If the build does not compile anymore, this is almost certainly a sign that
the upstream project is not yet ready for numpy 2.0; do not close this PR until
a version compatible with numpy 2.0 has been released upstream and on this
feedstock (in the meantime, you can keep the bot from reopening this PR in

+ +## Abstract + +This CEP aims to define the cache output for v1 multi-output recipes. + +## Background + +Sometimes it is very useful to build some code once, and then split it into multiple build artifacts (such as shared library, header files, etc.). For this reason, `conda-build` has a special, implicit top-level build. + +There are many downsides to the behavior of `conda-build`: it's very implicit, hard to understand and hard to debug (for example, if an output is defined with the same name as the top-level recipe, this output will get the same requirements attached as the top-level). + +For the v1 spec we are attempting to formalize the workings of the "top-level" build. For this, we introduce a new top-level key `cache`, that has the same values as a regular output. + +## Specification + +The top-level `cache` key looks as follows: + +```yaml +cache: + requirements: + build: + - ${{ compiler('c') }} + - cmake + - ninja + host: + - libzlib + # run: ... + # run_constraints: ... + # ignore_run_exports: ... + build: + # note: in the current implementation, all other keys for build + # are also valid, but unused + script: build.sh +``` + +
+ script build.sh default discussion +We had some debate wether the cache output should _also_ default to `build.sh` or should not have any default value for the `script`. This is still undecided. +
+ +When computing variants and used variables, rattler-build looks at the union of a given output and the cache. That means, even if an output does not define any requirements, the cache would still add a variant for the `c_compiler`. + +When rattler-build executes the recipe, it will start by building the cache output that is appropriate for the current variant. This is computed by looking at all "used-variables" for the cache output and computing a "hash" for the cache. The build itself is executed in the same way as any other build. + +The variant keys that are injected at build time is the subset used by the cache output. + +When the cache build is done, the newly created files are moved outside of the `host-prefix`. Post-processing is not performed on the files beyond memoizing what files contain the `$PREFIX` (which is later replaced in binaries and text files with the actual build-prefix with a simple 1-to-1 replacement as the prefix-length are guaranteed to be equal). + +The cache _only_ restores files that were added to the prefix (conda-build also restored source files). ## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))
  instead of marking packages as broken. This alternative workflow makes environments more reproducible.
* Packages with requirements/metadata that are too strict but otherwise work are
  not technically broken and should not be marked as such.
* Packages with missing metadata can be marked as broken on a temporary basis
  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.
* In some cases where the number of users of a package is small or it is used by
  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

What will happen when a package is marked broken?

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.

### Issue

Hello, thank you for supporting `aarch64` with conda-forge!

Unfortunately, the NCCL (Version 2.23.4) built for this PyTorch fails on our GH200 HPE Slingshot cluster. NCCL requires the use of our own provided `libfabric` and NCCL Plugin (https://github.com/aws/aws-ofi-nccl). PyTorch statically links to NCCL so while I cannot modify the NCCL used I can add the plugin without rebuilding from source.

I installed this conda env file:

```yaml
name: pytorch_env
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - nodefaults
dependencies:
  - python=3.10
  - pytorch=2.5.1
  - torchvision
  - transformers
```


# Replicate

I tried to execute a 2 node benchmark with the NCCL backend. However, it fails:

```python
import torch
from transformers import BertTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
import torch.distributed as dist
import time
import os

def init_process(backend='nccl'): # change to 'nccl' to use NCCL backend
    dist.init_process_group(backend=backend) 
    torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ['LOCAL_RANK']))

    if dist.get_rank() == 0:
        print(f"Initializing process group with backend: {backend}")
        num_cuda_devices = torch.cuda.device_count()
        print(f"Number of available CUDA devices: {num_cuda_devices}")
        world_size = dist.get_world_size()
        print(f"World size (number of processes in the process group): {world_size}")


def benchmark():
    # Load pre-trained model and tokenizer
    model_name = "bert-base-uncased"
    tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name).cuda()
    model = DDP(model, device_ids=[int(os.environ['LOCAL_RANK'])])

    # Prepare some sample text and labels
    texts = ["This is a sample sentence for benchmarking BERT."] * 32  # Batch of 32 sentences
    inputs = tokenizer(texts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True).to('cuda')
    labels = torch.ones(32, dtype=torch.long).to('cuda')  # Dummy labels

    # Benchmarking
    start_time = time.time()

    # Forward pass
    outputs = model(**inputs, labels=labels)
    loss = outputs.loss

    # Backward pass
    loss.backward()

    end_time = time.time()

    if dist.get_rank() == 0:
        print(f"Time taken for one forward and backward pass: {end_time - start_time} seconds")
    dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    init_process()
    benchmark()
```

From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. They can be published to `main`, and only the "magic" package `_numpy_rc` needs to be under a different channel (under the opt-in `conda-forge/label/numpy_rc`) > Does channel_targets automatically change to `conda-forge numpy_rc` if `_numpy_rc` is pulled, somehow? Also, I can't see any numpy packages labelled `numpy_rc` on the [conda-forge channel](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/numpy/labels), and I can see rc versions being uploaded [without a `numpy_rc` label](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/numpy/files). How this works is that: ``` conda install numpy=2.2.0rc1 # fails due to missing dependency _numpy_rc conda install -c conda-forge/label/numpy_rc numpy=2.2.0rc1 # succeeds ``` This isn't necessary per se for pytorch, but it's a less intrusive approach to handle rc-builds IMO (at the cost of having an extra magic package). {"action":"created","issue":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock/issues/310","repository_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock","labels_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock/issues/310/labels{/name}","comments_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock/issues/310/comments","events_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock/issues/310/events","html_url":"https://github.com/conda-forge/clangdev-feedstock/issues/310","id":2485640225,"node_id":"I_kwDOBLv6686UJ9wh","number":310,"title":"Newer libcxx versions obsoleting old clang versions","user":{"login":"h-vetinari","id":33685575,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjMzNjg1NTc1","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/33685575?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari","html_url":"https://github.com/h-vetinari","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/h-vetinari/received_events","type":"User","user_view_type":"public","site_admin":false},"labels":[],"state":"open","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":13,"created_at":"2024-08-26T01:33:47Z","updated_at":"2024-12-07T23:51:44Z","closed_at":null,"author_association":"MEMBER","sub_issues_summary":{"total":0,"completed":0,"percent_completed":0},"active_lock_reason":null,"body":"This is a long-standing problem. Upstream libcxx generally only supports the last two released clang versions (during development), meaning libcxx 18 only officially supports clang 16 & 17 (and of course 18 once released).

As libcxx is generally highly forward-compatible, we only ever have one libcxx version in conda-forge, which tends to be the newest. Strictly speaking, the C++ compilers on osx only do a run-export on their own version, so `clangxx_ox-64 17.0.6` will produce packages that have a `libcxx >=17` [constraint](https://github.com/conda-forge/clang-compiler-activation-feedstock/blob/52e3513c4592a367930372717c22cc5fb680d133/recipe/meta.yaml#L115). Once we update our compiler stack to a new LLVM version, this constraint spreads pretty quickly across the ecosystem, so that a requirement for an older libcxx is effectively equivalent to freezing the set of packages/versions that remain co-installable.

We do [test](https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-testing-feedstock) our libcxx against older clangs, and for example, libcxx 17 passes basic [testing](https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-feedstock/blob/e7a3470896a9ae4b598d31e3fcd94fda729055d3/recipe/meta.yaml#L107-L118) all the way down to clang 11 (and even 10 still [worked](https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-testing-feedstock/pull/5#issuecomment-1675740688)). That's for the most basic include tests, i.e. it needs to be said that there are almost certainly bugs in other parts of libcxx in that combination (as libcxx 17 only supports down to clang 15 officially, and usually removes all workarounds that are necessary for older clangs). However, it seems this setup has worked +/- acceptably for affected packages so far.

For libcxx 18, we ended up [dropping](https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-feedstock/commit/a09b2d6b37dfa64ee4f71da0926be34fcc87e13c) support for clang<15, after checking the status of some known packages that are still relying on older clang:

> [Decide](https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-feedstock/pull/155) what to do (if anything) about losing support for clang<15 -> drop
>  * root moved on to clang 16
>  * cling is not maintained anymore (quoth @SylvainCorlay)
>  * llvmlite still at llvm 14, but that does not conflict with newer clang/libcxx

This is not yet an immediate concern because our default compilers aren't on clang 18 yet, but we'll run into the same situation once that happens, so this is to serve as an announcement & for discussion; c.f. also #309, where I commented:

<details>

>  This is OK by me. It should also be possible though to stay on clang 16 in `cppyy-cling`; you're not forced to follow the global pinning, and you have very good reason (currently) not to. One issue with that is of course that other packages being installed today pick up the `libcxx>=17` requirement, so this PR is necessary for staying co-installable with packages currently being built.
>
> Looking forward, root already has a 16.x version (and I see you've tried it in that PR, but cppyy doesn't support it yet), which is good, because when we move to LLVM 18, clang 13 won't work with libcxx 18 anymore (https://github.com/conda-forge/libcxx-feedstock/commit/a09b2d6b37dfa64ee4f71da0926be34fcc87e13c). We can maybe forestall the change for a while (or keep using libcxx 17 with the clang 18 compilers for a bit), but past some point, it'll always come down to either: switch to newer clang versions, or live with old packages in the environment.
>
> We try to keep libcxx compatible with older clang versions much longer than upstream LLVM, but there are limits to how far we can push this, and ultimately the tide doesn't stop rising. 🥲

```
conda install -c conda-forge python-freethreading numpy
```
what gets populated is
```
$PREFIX/lib/python3.13t/site-packages/{numpy,...}  # including all the built-in imports
$PREFIX/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pip           # and presumably other noarch packages
```

However, when trying to build something on top (e.g. scipy), `SP_DIR` for the free-threading builds doesn't match the main site-package directory (`python3.13` instead of `python3.13t`) and so the build fails[^1]

[^1]: I'm not talking about the `pip install`, which works fine (and installs into `python3.13t`), but we need to manually [copy something](https://github.com/conda-forge/scipy-feedstock/blob/9fe7f7450dc83b1b366dfafc3a335238103d1951/recipe/build-output.sh#L9) to `$SP_DIR/scipy`, due to the way the tests get split off into their own package.

Not sure what's the best approach here, but my understanding would be that this is simply a bug that `SP_DIR` needs to reflect the `t` for freethreading builds.

Notes and instructions for merging this PR: 1. Please merge the PR only after the tests have passed. 2. Feel free to push to the bot's branch to update this PR if needed. **Please note that if you close this PR we presume that the feedstock has been rebuilt, so if you are going to perform the rebuild yourself don't close this PR until the your rebuild has been merged.**
Here are some more details about this specific migrator: > > TL;DR: We are trying to switch our Fortran compilers on windows to flang. > This is not 100% guaranteed to work, but should be fine in the majority of cases. > > The new LLVM-based flang has become mature enough that it should be possible to > broadly switch over our Fortran compilers on windows to it (until now we only had > an ancient pre-LLVM flang 5, or alternatively the GCC-based `m2w64_fortran`). > > As such, this PR attempts to homogenize any use of `m2w64_fortran` and other `m2w64_*` > compilers to our default stack (which would then be MSVC + flang on windows), with > the exception of feedstocks for R-packages, which stay on the `m2w64_` compilers. > > Recipes that have hard-coded expectations about the name of the fortran compiler > will need to adjust to use `%FC%` or `flang-new` for the compiler name. ### Issue

Dear maintainer:

I'm not quite sure whether this is the correct place to report this bug.

I'm trying to use cmake's [FindBLAS](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindBLAS.html) to find the openblas installed in a conda virtual environment in a very old cluster (centos 7), but it fails with this reason:

```
/export/home/myname/miniconda3/envs/gfortran-test/bin/../lib/gcc/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/14.2.0/../../../../x86_64-conda-linux-gnu/bin/ld: /export/home/myname/miniconda3/envs/gfortran-test/lib/libopenblas.so: undefined reference to `memcpy@GLIBC_2.14'
```

here is the minimal example to reproduce the error:

```console
$ conda create -n gfortran-test
$ conda activate gfortran-test
$ conda install -c conda-forge cmake gfortran openblas "libopenblas=*=*openmp*"
$ which cmake
/export/home/myname/miniconda3/envs/gfortran-test/bin/cmake
$ which gfortran
/export/home/myname/miniconda3/envs/gfortran-test/bin/gfortran
$ cat CMakeLists.txt # this is the content of CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25)

project(test VERSION 0.1 LANGUAGES Fortran)

set(BLA_VENDOR "OpenBLAS")
find_package(BLAS REQUIRED)
$ FC=gfortran cmake -S . -B build
```

Notice that cmake can not find the openblas installed.

I trace the cmake process and hacked the `~/miniconda3/envs/gfortran-test/share/cmake-3.31/Modules/CheckFortranFunctionExists.cmake` (this is where the `FindBLAS` fails) to print the fail reason:

Below a list of deprecations by kind and scipy release. Ideally all _**deprecations should come with an announced behaviour change, and with an announced timeframe**_ (i.e. SciPy version where things will be changed/removed), and other items migrated there as appropriate.

In most cases, we aim for removal/behaviour change _one year_ after a given deprecation is introduced in `1.N` (not just in documentation, but in a way that the user cannot miss, i.e. raise DeprecationWarning upon use). Due to the 6 month release cadence this often ends up being `1.(N+2)`, but exceptional out-of-band releases can occur, so try to avoid promising exact versions. For more disruptive cases, adaptations (e.g. longer timeframes) can be made as necessary.

> [!IMPORTANT]  
> If you add newly-deprecated functionality to the tracker, please do so _twice_ - once for tracking what we did for the upcoming release (whether following up on old doc-only deprecation or completely new deprecations), and once for tracking when that deprecation is scheduled to be executed (generally two releases later).

### Removal announced for 1.16

<!-- Please formulate these as follow-up actions, not just links to a PR that does a deprecation (which should go under "New deprecations" for the upcoming release) -->

Open issues for these once 1.15 branches off of `main`.

* 1.14
  * remove `conjtransp()` from dok_array/matrix classes (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20283))
  * remove support for masked arrays from `power_divergence` and `chisquare` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20753))
  * remove support for `quadrature='trapz'` from `integrate.quad_vec` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20716))
  * raise error for non-integer types with `exact=True` in `special.comb` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20780))
  * remove one-arg use for `stats.linregress` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20789))
  * raise error for non-integer types with `exact=True` in `special.perm` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20909))



### Removal announced for 1.17

<!-- Please formulate these as follow-up actions, not just links to a PR that does a deprecation (which should go under "New deprecations" for the upcoming release) -->

* 1.15
  * remove `rand` and `seed` functions from `scipy.linalg.interpolative` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20558))
  * raise an error for complex inputs to `spatial.{cosine,correlation}` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21085))
  * remove `scipy.stats.find_repeats` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21157))
  * remove support for object arrays and longdoubles in `signal.{correlate,convolve,lfilter,sosfilter}` (follow-up to [this](gh-21211) and [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21706)
  * remove `scipy.linalg.kron` (follow-up to [this](gh-21633))
  * remove `kulczynski1` and `sokalmichener` metrics from `spatial.distance` (follow-up to [this](gh-21572))
  *  Remove ravelling of inputs in `linalg.toeplitz` (follow-up to [this](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21446))

You've moved the dependencies to the output, but haven't moved the build-script (and actually, you should move the `python: noarch` too, and add it to `scipy-typed` as well). Note that conda-recipes have an implicit "global" output (named after `package: name: ...`), and if this coincides with an output name, this results in very unintuitive behaviour (https://github.com/conda/conda-build/issues/4172). Standard fix is to rename the package-name into something not conflicting (e.g. `scipy-stubs-split`), and then add ```diff extra: recipe-maintainers: - lucascolley - jorenham + feedstock-name: scipy-stubs ``` Sidenote: you should also get rid of the templating on `name` - it's completely pointless (the package name cannot be changed), and creates both extra mental overhead plus more opportunities for bugs. PS. You'll also need to rename the script if you want to run it in the output itself (using `script: .sh`), because `build.sh` is a reserved name that will _always_ be executed in the recipe-global build stage, which isn't doing anything here anymore. PPS. There's a way to keep using the existing setup despite adding another output, but it's rather confusing, so I don't recommend doing it... It would entail adding a single-line `output: scipy-typed` (in this case explicitly repeating `package: name: ...`) like ```yaml outputs: - name: scipy-stubs # nothing else! - name: scipy-typed [...] ``` but to actually test this output, you'd have to specify the `test:` section before `outputs:`.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/conda-forge/scipy-stubs-feedstock/issues/comments/2526413501/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

Hi!

Thank you for making an admin request on this repo. We strive to make a decision
on these requests within 24 hours.

Please use the text below to add context about this PR, especially if:
- You want to mark packages as broken
- You want to archive a feedstock
- You want to request access to opt-in CI resources

Cheers and thank you for contributing to conda-forge!
-->

## Guidelines for marking packages as broken:

* We prefer to patch the repo data (see [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-repodata-patches-feedstock))
  instead of marking packages as broken. This alternative workflow makes environments more reproducible.
* Packages with requirements/metadata that are too strict but otherwise work are
  not technically broken and should not be marked as such.
* Packages with missing metadata can be marked as broken on a temporary basis
  but should be patched in the repo data and be marked unbroken later.
* In some cases where the number of users of a package is small or it is used by
  the maintainers only, we can allow packages to be marked broken more liberally.
* We (`conda-forge/core`) try to make a decision on these requests within 24 hours.

What will happen when a package is marked broken?

* Our bots will add the `broken` label to the package. The `main` label will remain on the package and this is normal.
* Our bots will rebuild our repodata patches to remove this package from the repodata.
* In a few hours after the `anaconda.org` CDN picks up the new patches, you will no longer be able to install the package from the `main` channel.


## Checklist:

* [ ] I want to mark a package as broken (or not broken):
  * [ ] Added a description of the problem with the package in the PR description.
  * [ ] Pinged the team for the package for their input.

* [ ] I want to archive a feedstock:
  * [ ] Pinged the team for that feedstock for their input.
  * [ ] Make sure you have opened an issue on the feedstock explaining why it was archived.
  * [ ] Linked that issue in this PR description.
  * [ ] Added links to any other relevant issues/PRs in the PR description.

* [ ] I want to request (or revoke) access to an opt-in CI resource:
  * [ ] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [ ] Added a small description explaining why access is needed

* [ ] I want to copy an artifact following [CFEP-3](https://github.com/conda-forge/cfep/blob/main/cfep-03.md):
  * [ ] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [ ] Added a reference to the original PR
  * [ ] Posted a link to the conda artifacts
  * [ ] Posted a link to the build logs

* [ ] I want to add a package output to a feedstock:
  * [ ] Pinged the relevant feedstock team(s)
  * [ ] Added a small description of why the output is being added.

<!--
For example if you are trying to mark a `foo` conda package as broken.

  ping @conda-forge/foo

-->

request came up a number of times, e.g. in #15480 (also discussed in #15600 and #18409). Since #18409 focused primarily on the complex extension, I'm opening a separate issue for implementing the recurrence relation for `factorial2` -- that is, in case there's sufficient interest.

This is a different extension of the double-factorial which returns finite values for negative integers (as opposed to `0` for `extend='zero'`), based on [inverting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_factorial#Negative_arguments) the recurrence relation:
```
(n+2)!! = (n + 2) * n!!
```
to give the following for odd positive n:
```
(-n)!! = (-1) ** ((n-1)/2) * n / n!!
       = (-1) ** ((n-1)/2) / (n-2)!!
```

I'm not 100% sure what to do with other negative values, presumably this should raise a `ValueError` for any input that's not an integer (and likewise if `exact` isn't `True`), and return `np.inf` or `np.nan` for negative even integers.

Interestingly, the complex extension from #21801 already seems to match the values implied by the recurrence relation, so from that POV we may also decide that this is something we do not need to support explicitly:
```python
>>> from scipy.special import *
>>> factorial2(-1, extend="complex")
np.float64(0.9999999999999999)          #  1    =  1/1   =  1/1!!
>>> factorial2(-3, extend="complex")
np.float64(-0.9999999999999999)         # -1    = -3/3   = -3/3!! = -1/(3-2)!!
>>> factorial2(-5, extend="complex")
np.float64(0.33333333333333337)         #  1/3  =  5/15  =  5/5!! =  1/(5-2)!!
>>> factorial2(-7, extend="complex")
np.float64(-0.06666666666666667)        # -1/15 = -7/105 = -7/7!! = -1/(7-2)!!
```

In principle, the same extension technique should also be applicable to `factorialk` at negative integers (except against for negative multiples of `k`, i.e. the poles), though presumably the complex extension there already provides a decent approximation as well.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/scipy/scipy/issues/21874/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"timeline_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/scipy/scipy/issues/21874/timeline","performed_via_github_app":null,"state_reason":"completed"}}

From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. In the end, we are only grabbing a handful of files for `libtorch*` packages and they are in predictable location in the build directory. `pip install` remains being used in the final builds for `pytorch`. From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. In the end, we are only grabbing a handful of files for `libtorch*` packages and they are in predictable location in the build directory. `pip install` remains being used in the final builds for `pytorch`. From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. Comment:

With rolling out flang 19 for all Fortran packages on conda-forge, is there a strategy for enabling ABI compatibility for Fortran packages which are using Fortran modules?

In practice, a Fortran project currently using `{{ compiler('m2w64_fortran') }}` (gfortran 14) can only consume Fortran dependencies which are also build with the same compiler. The current migration might lead to situations where a dependency is build with `{{ compiler('fortran') }}` (flang 19) and than used as dependency for a package which expects the gfortran ABI. As example the flang ABI uses a different name mangling for symbols in Fortran modules. Furthermore, module files generated by flang are generally not readable by gfortran and vice versa.

It would be great to have a transition phase where Fortran projects using modules can be built with both ABIs (gfortran and flang) without having the risk of mixing and breaking packages while migrating from gfortran to flang as a compiler on From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. In the end, we are only grabbing a handful of files for `libtorch*` packages and they are in predictable location in the build directory. `pip install` remains being used in the final builds for `pytorch`. From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. In the end, we are only grabbing a handful of files for `libtorch*` packages and they are in predictable location in the build directory. `pip install` remains being used in the final builds for `pytorch`. Is this based on your experience or facts? It's based on @rgommers' statement "10 or so functions, vs. [...] all of libtorch". I don't know pytorch nearly as well as Ralf, so I caveated my point with "assuming their percentage [of those who need it] among users is reasonably small". IMO it's always a numbers game (and often we don't know the numbers, so we stay conservative; which is fine!) - if we knew, say, that <0.1% of users are affected, then burdening 99.9% users with a useless 2GB download sounds unappealing. The question gets progressively harder the higher we estimate the percentage. Probably anything north of 5% of users, we'd default to performance rather than footprint? I don't have a magic bullet. 🤷 > provide the same features as in upstream conda/wheels so that users who do use our packages are not driven away by mysterious performance issues. I agree with the overall direction of course. We still have a few things to catch up (e.g. cpuarch builds, as IIUC pytorch effectively [requires](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.5.1/cmake/MiscCheck.cmake#L42-L48) something between x86_64 v3 and v4). That said, it's certainly technically possible to warn users of a potential performance-cliff where we don't yet support certain upstream optimizations (or require an opt-in for whatever reason). It's mainly a question of how much of that we want to patch and/or upstream. To be clear, I'm also OK with "fat binaries are preferable to performance degradation or extra maintenance effort". The magma-case is just not so black-and-white IMO. What do you think about the idea of making an exception to link libmagma From the commit message: Upstream keeps all magma-related routines in a separate libtorch_cuda_linalg library that is loaded dynamically whenever linalg functions are used. Given the library is relatively small, splitting it makes it possible to provide "magma" and "nomagma" variants that can be alternated between. Also: Try to speed up magma/nomagma builds a bit. Rather than rebuilding the package 3 times (possibly switching magma → nomagma → magma again), build it twice at the very beginning and store the built files for later reuse in subpackage builds. While at it, replace the `pip wheel` calls with `setup.py build` to avoid unnecessarily zipping up and then unpacking the whole thing. In the end, we are only grabbing a handful of files for `libtorch*` packages and they are in predictable location in the build directory. `pip install` remains being used in the final builds for `pytorch`. the context of the BLAS variant [testing](https://github.com/conda-forge/scipy-feedstock/pull/273) for scipy, I noticed that the OpenBLAS runs were much slower. I did some basic timing comparisons based on what pytest reports as the overall runtime of the scipy test suite (the timing _also_ depends quite a bit on whether the agent has AVX512F/AVX512CD or not, and this is random across Azure's fleet, so I'm taking the average across implementation & CPU type):

| Flavour | Avg. (AVX2) | \#runs | Avg. (AVX512) | \#runs |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| blis | 00:26:10.0 | 2 | 00:18:28.2 | 6 |
| mkl | 00:24:35.4 | 5 | 00:18:56.4 | 5 |
| netlib | 00:25:44.7 | 3 | 00:19:03.0 | 5 |
| openblas | 01:34:15.0 | 2 | 01:24:06.8 | 4 | 

Overall, OpenBLAS ends up being between 3-5x slower than all the other BLAS/LAPACK implementations, which to me is indicative of something going very wrong somewhere.

it's taken us so long to upgrade from centOS 6 to 7, we'll very quickly find ourselves in a situation that we struggled with already some time ago (see discussion in this [issue](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge.github.io/issues/1436)): a growing number of feedstocks will require a newer glibc, and our images should provide a new enough baseline version, so that the only thing that feedstocks need to actively override is `c_stdlib_version` (and thus the sysroot), but nothing else.

For example, google's "foundational" support matrix [defines](https://github.com/google/oss-policies-info/blob/0c6d8dfaf4bb48ec2505c79b9825b4986e1f1ebe/foundational-cxx-support-matrix.md?plain=1#L24) a lower bound of glibc 2.27, meaning that things like abseil/bazel/grpc/protobuf/re2 etc. will start beginning to rely on glibc features >2.17 in the near future (and even though it's not a google project, one of the baseline dependencies of that stack is [starting](https://github.com/conda-forge/c-ares-feedstock/pull/38) to require it).

We can handle the `c_stdlib_version` in the migrators (like we [did](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge-pinning-feedstock/blob/a9c6bf9af2f75c46aaeeda445c87cec43970aeb4/recipe/migrations/libabseil20230802_libgrpc157_libprotobuf4234.yaml#L1-L10) for macOS 10.13, before the conda-forge-wide baseline was lifted), but changing more than one key of the mega-zip involving the docker images is really painful, especially if CUDA is involved ([example](https://github.com/conda-forge/faiss-split-feedstock/blob/a329d1efab47efb466050dbaea52b5d26876649d/recipe/conda_build_config.yaml#L1-L35)), so having the images be alma8 by default will be very helpful there.

To a lesser extent, it will also save us from run-time bugs in older glibc versions, like we had with some broken trigonometry functions in 2.12 (before the image moved to cos7 while the sysroot still stayed at 2.12).

There are other scenarios still where this is necessary, see the discussion [here](https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge.github.io/pull/2206#discussion_r1674100297) for example.

While it's already possible to use alma8 images, the main thing we're blocked is the lack of CDTs for alma 8 (pending https://github.com/conda-forge/cdt-builds/issues/66), c.f. https://github.com/conda-forge/conda-forge.github.io/issues/1941

This issue is for tracking this effort, and any other eventual tasks that need to be resolved before doing so.
